strengths: Well-motivated research question addressing whether learned 3D reconstruction models capture geometric principles or rely on data priors—timely and important for understanding modern foundation models
Comprehensive multi-faceted analysis combining probing classifiers, attention visualization, causal interventions via knockout, and robustness evaluation under systematic perturbations
Controlled synthetic dataset from ShapeNet with precise control over camera configurations, lighting, focal length, and object symmetry enables rigorous isolation of specific phenomena

Clear empirical progression showing epipolar geometry emerges in middle layers, correlates with correspondence matching in attention heads, and exhibits causal relationship to specific layer-head combinations

Extensive robustness evaluation comparing against classical methods (SIFT+RANSAC, SuperGlue+RANSAC) across diverse challenging scenarios (occlusions, lighting/color variations, focal length changes, symmetric objects)
Honest discussion of limitations including synthetic-only data, non-local interventions, inability to claim specific algorithm implementation, and potentially unwanted hallucination behavior
Detailed reproducibility information in main text and comprehensive supplementary materials with dataset generation procedures and additional experimental details
weaknesses: Exclusive reliance on synthetic ShapeNet data evaluated with Blender rendering; while enabling control, severely limits generalizability claims given VGGT was trained on diverse real-world datasets—lacks any real-image validation

Causal intervention analysis uses coarse method (zeroing entire attention maps for layer-head combinations); supplementary Figs. 13-14 show localized interventions yield dramatically weaker effects (0.2-10.2 vs. 71.7 pixel increases), substantially qualifying causal claims that correspondence matching drives epipolar geometry

Hallucination behavior (model maintains ~50% correspondence matching on occluded patches) identified as 'potentially undesirable' but inadequately explored—lacks investigation of when/why it occurs, its actual impact on reconstruction accuracy, and mitigation strategies

Fundamental matrix probing methodology is indirect; trains MLPs on camera tokens rather than verifying F is actually used for predictions; no ablation distinguishing whether performance stems from learned geometry vs. learned F structure priors; limited to single geometric property (F)

Missing functional understanding: paper demonstrates F representation emerges and responds to attention knockouts, but does not establish why F matters functionally for VGGT's actual training objectives (camera pose, depth, point cloud, tracking) or whether disrupting F degrades these main tasks

Robustness claims partially overstated: VGGT shows 25.1% failure under asymmetric top-view lighting (comparable to baselines), performs on par with classical methods for stereo pairs, and demonstrates clear advantage mainly for large viewpoint differences—scenario-dependent rather than universally superior

Limited dataset scope: only 10-13 ShapeNet categories, mostly texture-rich simple objects; acknowledged that SIFT struggles with synthetic data confounding relative performance conclusions; symmetric object experiments use artificial repetitive arrangements not representative of real complexity

Incomplete geometric analysis: only probes epipolar geometry; does not investigate camera intrinsics recovery, rotation/translation decomposition, or 3D triangulation; narrow scope of geometric properties examined
No detailed comparison with concurrent work (Stary et al. [25] on DUSt3R); unclear whether discovered geometric structure generalizes to other 3D foundation models or is VGGT-specific

Probing and testing use same synthetic distribution (different splits); potential for encoding dataset-specific statistics rather than true geometric understanding; lacks analysis of VGGT training objectives and whether geometric learning was explicitly encouraged
Small test sets (5-40 scenes for different experiments) without reported confidence intervals or statistical significance testing on key metrics; hyperparameter choices for MLP probes not justified

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question about whether learned 3D models implicitly capture fundamental geometric principles, filling a gap in interpretability research for 3D vision

Comprehensive multi-faceted methodology combining probing, attention analysis, and causal interventions with progressive refinement (Figures 4, 13-14) that triangulates findings beyond any single approach

Clear and striking empirical finding that epipolar geometry emerges around layer 12 with consonance to correspondence matching emergence at layer 10, well-demonstrated across multiple evaluation splits
Thoughtfully designed controlled synthetic dataset from ShapeNet with complete ground truth enabling precise analysis of geometric properties across camera configurations and focal lengths

Systematic robustness evaluation revealing VGGT's superior handling of occlusions and scene perturbations compared to classical methods, with interesting finding that ~50% of matching heads persist under occlusion

Rigorous progression of interventions from global attention knockout to correspondence-specific intervention, properly acknowledging limitations and demonstrating genuine causality rather than mere correlation
weaknesses: Critical generalization concern: all experiments use synthetic ShapeNet data despite VGGT being trained on diverse real-world datasets; lack of even small-scale real-image validation severely limits confidence that findings characterize actual model behavior in deployment

Overstated claims conflating 'linear probe can recover fundamental matrix' with 'model encodes epipolar geometry'; linear separability of representations does not demonstrate explicit geometric reasoning, and no analysis of what computational operations actually implement epipolar constraints

Incomplete causal evidence: Figures 13-14 show substantially weaker degradation with localized interventions (10.2px vs. 71.7px), contradicting the hypothesis that correspondence matching alone drives epipolar geometry and suggesting other unidentified mechanisms in these heads

Underdeveloped analysis of 'learned data priors' despite being central to title and abstract; concept remains vague and mechanistically unexplored; occlusion hallucinations dismissed without investigation; robustness to appearance variations likely stems from training augmentations but not analyzed

Limited methodological novelty: applies established techniques (probing classifiers, attention visualization, activation patching) without introducing new interpretability methods, reducing contribution for a top-tier venue

Missing critical ablations: no investigation of how geometric emergence changes when correspondences aren't supervised; no factorization of which training objectives drive emergence; no analysis of architectural effects (transformers vs. alternatives)
Statistical rigor concerns: occlusion experiments use only ~40 scenes without significance testing or error quantification; asymmetric attention acknowledged but not investigated (Figure 11)

Restricted experimental scope: simple synthetic scenes with isolated objects and controlled lighting fail to reflect real-world geometric complexity; brief dismissal of concurrent work (Stary et al., 2025); SIFT comparison confounded by synthetic dataset properties

Limited practical impact: doesn't improve models, propose architectural modifications, develop methods, or advance theory; value is primarily intellectual without actionable insights for improving 3D reconstruction pipelines

Presentation: conflates 'representation sufficiency for geometric computation' with explicit 'understanding' throughout; heatmaps in Figures 3, 11 are difficult to parse; 'learned priors' concept should be operationalized upfront rather than vaguely referenced

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question about whether deep learning models for 3D reconstruction learn explicit geometric principles or rely on learned priors, which is crucial for understanding generalization
Systematic and rigorous multi-pronged methodology combining probing, attention analysis, and causal interventions that progresses logically from correlational to causal claims
Excellent experimental design using synthetic data with complete ground truth, enabling precise control over scene properties and eliminating confounds that would complicate interpretability analysis

Clear and well-supported findings with appropriate caveats: epipolar geometry emerges in middle layers, correspondence matching precedes geometry, and causal links are established between attention patterns and geometric understanding
Thorough robustness evaluation across diverse conditions (occlusions, lighting, symmetry, focal length) comparing VGGT against classical methods, revealing both capabilities and failure modes

Methodological rigor with transparency about limitations: uses public VGGT checkpoint, provides detailed dataset/implementation specifications, progressively refines interventions from global to localized (appendices), and clearly acknowledges limitations
Excellent presentation with clear writing, logical organization, informative visualizations, and comprehensive supplementary material
Well-motivated application of interpretability methods to 3D geometric vision, contributing methodology that could be applied to other models
weaknesses: All experiments conducted on synthetic ShapeNet data; generalization to real images is unvalidated. VGGT was trained on natural images with different statistics, so the relevance of synthetic findings to understanding real-world behavior remains unclear

Causal analysis has limitations: main paper interventions (Fig. 4) zero out entire attention maps affecting multiple potential mechanisms, and even localized interventions (appendix) cannot definitively isolate correspondence matching as the causal mechanism. Causal claims in abstract are somewhat overstated

Analysis scope is narrow, focusing only on epipolar geometry via fundamental matrix. VGGT predicts multiple outputs (camera parameters, depth, point tracks), and the connection between encoded epipolar geometry and end-to-end task performance is unexplored

Important finding about hallucinations under occlusion (Section 5.1: ~50% correspondence retention for occluded patches) is identified but under-explored. Missing investigation of hallucination quality, semantic coherence, and impact on downstream predictions

Limited baseline comparisons: only SIFT+RANSAC and SuperGlue+RANSAC compared; no comparison with other recent learned models (DUSt3R, MASt3R). Concurrent work by Stary et al. on DUSt3R is mentioned but not compared, limiting evidence for generality

Probing methodology uses simple 2-layer MLPs; known limitation that shallow probes may miss non-linear structure and don't necessarily indicate the model uses or interprets the information. Missing non-linear probes or information-theoretic measures

Scope limited to 2-view pairs and specific camera configurations on ShapeNet; generalization to multi-view scenarios and arbitrary configurations unclear. Whether insights are VGGT-specific or general to other learned geometry models is unknown

Missing ablations on alternative geometric quantities (essential matrix, epipoles, etc.), probe architectures, and analysis of how multi-task training influences geometric understanding. Limited investigation of failure modes (e.g., failures on asymmetric lighting in Fig. 6)

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated research question about whether modern 3D reconstruction models learn fundamental geometric principles or rely primarily on learned data-based priors

Comprehensive and systematic analysis across three representative models (DUSt3R, VGGT, DA3) using multiple complementary techniques: probing for geometric quantities, attention analysis, causal interventions, and robustness testing
Excellent experimental design with controlled synthetic dataset (ShapeNet-based) providing precise control over scene properties, enabling rigorous systematic assessment

Clear and well-supported findings demonstrated through multiple perspectives: all models encode epipolar geometry in intermediate layers, correspondence matching emerges via attention mechanisms, and models maintain geometric consistency despite missing evidence
Exceptional presentation quality with well-designed, informative figures that effectively communicate complex analytical findings and support clear conclusions
Thorough coverage including analysis across real-world datasets (DTU, ETH3D, MipNeRF360), semantic correspondences, feature similarity, model size effects, and focal length variations
weaknesses: Limited novelty in analytical methodology: probing for geometric quantities, attention analysis, and attention knockout interventions are standard interpretability techniques applied rather than novel methods developed

Causality claims may be overstated: demonstrating that intervening on attention heads degrads performance establishes correlation but not strict causation; potential redundancy in learned representations and alternative pathways not thoroughly examined

Limited theoretical insight into underlying mechanisms: paper identifies empirical patterns but provides insufficient explanation for why these representations emerge or how learned priors and geometric consistency mechanistically interact

Incomplete coverage and limited generalization: results for DA3 are restricted (only valid cases for some interventions); findings primarily from clean datasets; limited exploration of extremely challenging real-world scenarios; generalization to other architectures unclear

Practical implications unclear: paper diagnoses that models learn geometric structure and depend on learned priors but does not provide strong actionable guidance for improving future model design or addressing identified limitations

Experimental rigor concerns: lack of statistical significance testing and confidence intervals; some results from single epochs; occlusion experiments use only simple masking; focal length variations test limited range

Under-exploration of important findings: symmetric scenes and geometric ambiguity (Section E.2) where classical methods fail are intriguing but insufficiently analyzed with respect to deployment reliability

Missing systematic comparisons: limited direct comparison between classical geometry-based methods and learned representations; contrast between geometric reasoning and learned priors could be more explicit

strengths: Addresses an important research question about the interplay between geometric principles and learned priors in modern 3D reconstruction models
Comprehensive and systematic experimental design with careful ablations, multiple datasets, and multiple analysis perspectives (geometric, attentional, data-driven)
Clear empirical findings demonstrated through well-designed probing experiments showing epipolar geometry emergence in middle layers across models
Effective visualizations that clearly communicate where geometric patterns emerge in networks and across different model types
Balanced and nuanced interpretation that avoids overstating claims about geometric understanding vs. learned priors
weaknesses: Limited novelty as a contribution type: This is primarily an analysis/interpretability paper with no new algorithms, architectures, or methods—it characterizes existing models rather than advancing state-of-the-art
Lack of actionable insights: Findings are intellectually interesting but provide no clear guidance on designing better models, improving robustness, or practical implications for practitioners
Causality claims insufficiently supported: Attention knockout experiments show correlation but don't definitively prove causation. Alternative mechanisms could produce similar observations
Limitations of interpretability methodology: MLP probing success doesn't definitively show what information is actually used by models. Simple cosine similarity metrics may miss complex relationships
Vague characterization of learned priors: While identifying reliance on learned priors, the paper provides limited insight into what these priors actually are or why they emerge

Limited scope: Only 3 recent transformer-based models analyzed; no comparison with other paradigms. Synthetic dataset is relatively simple. Generalizability to other architectures/training regimes unclear
Incomplete failure mode analysis: While robustness is discussed, analysis of when/why models fail remains superficial. Fully symmetric scene failure is interesting but underdeveloped
Statistical rigor lacking: Some figures lack error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs. No formal significance testing reported
Missing reproducibility resources: No mention of code availability. Some implementation details unclear (probe training details, convergence criteria, computational requirements)
Oversimplified causality arguments: Conflates 'decodable from representation' with 'actually used by model'—a known challenge in neural network interpretability

strengths: Addresses an important and timely scientific question: whether modern 3D reconstruction models encode fundamental geometric principles or rely primarily on learned priors

Exceptionally thorough experimental design spanning 3 representative models, multiple real-world and synthetic datasets, and diverse analysis techniques (probing, attention analysis, interventions, perturbations)
Rigorous methodology that distinguishes correlation from causation through well-designed attention-knockout interventions with proper experimental controls
Excellent visualization and clear presentation: figures effectively communicate where and how geometric information emerges in network layers
Comprehensive experimental transparency with detailed descriptions of hyperparameters, probe designs, and procedures supporting reproducibility; uses public datasets and models
Multi-faceted analysis perspective examining phenomena through geometric (fundamental matrix), data (correspondence matching), and semantic (feature similarity) lenses
Provides practical insights into model robustness properties and failure modes that inform design of more reliable 3D vision systems
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily an analysis/interpretation paper rather than proposing new methods or advancing state-of-the-art performance
Incomplete mechanistic understanding: shows WHERE geometry emerges (mid-layer attention heads) but provides limited insight into WHY or HOW this learning occurs
Limited model coverage: only 3 models analyzed; scope could be expanded to other paradigms and more recent architectures for stronger generalization claims
Incomplete characterization of robustness: occlusion tests limited to 2-image pairs; systematic perturbation analysis focuses primarily on focal length variations
Statistical rigor could be stronger: many results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests; some findings based on limited sampling
Limited actionable insights for practitioners: paper is descriptive but doesn't propose concrete architectural modifications or training strategies to improve existing methods

Analytical method limitations not fully addressed: MLP probe capacity effects on interpretability conclusions; potential artifacts from attention-knockout interventions; averaging across conditions may obscure variations
Dataset constraints: synthetic ShapeNet limited to controlled scenarios; real-world datasets relatively small; no systematic analysis of dataset bias effects on findings
Multi-view analysis only sketched for 2-view correspondence; extension to multi-view settings incomplete
Some technical details could be clearer: exact intervention procedures are somewhat sparse; probe optimization details and potential overfitting not thoroughly discussed
